displayQuote: To thine own self be true

meta.title: Who really said "To thine own self be true"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Scripture. Polonius says it in Shakespeare's Hamlet, Act 1, Scene 3 (c. 1599-1601). A King James search finds the phrase in no verse.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'To thine own self be true'?
meta.ogDescription: It's Shakespeare, not the Bible. The line is Polonius's, in Hamlet Act 1, Scene 3 - and it appears in no King James verse.

answer.label: Not the Bible — actually William Shakespeare
answer.authorDates: c. 1564–1616 · English playwright, poet and actor
answer.sourceLine: The line is Polonius’s, spoken to his son Laertes in Act 1, Scene 3 of Hamlet — a play written around 1599–1601 and first printed in quarto in 1603. The full sentence runs “This above all: to thine own self be true; / And it must follow, as the night the day, / Thou canst not then be false to any man.” It is not Scripture: a King James Version search for “thine own self” returns only Exodus 32:13 and Philemon 1:19, and neither contains the maxim.

docMeta.dd: Act 1, Scene 3 — Polonius’s farewell precepts to Laertes
c. 1599–1601; first printed in quarto 1603, second quarto 1604/5, First Folio 1623
Polonius, a character — not Shakespeare in his own voice

source.excerpt:
Neither a borrower nor a lender be:
For loan oft loses both itself and friend;
And borrowing dulls the edge of husbandry.
This above all: to thine own self be true;
And it must follow, as the night the day,
Thou canst not then be false to any man.
Farewell: my blessing season this in thee.
trail: The line sits at the close of Polonius’s speech of precepts to Laertes in Project Gutenberg’s text of Hamlet ↗, four lines after “Neither a borrower nor a lender be”.
Wikiquote’s Hamlet article ↗ assigns the quotation to Polonius at Act I, scene iii, with the two following lines attached.
A King James Version search for “thine own self” at Bible Gateway ↗ returns only Exodus 32:13 and Philemon 1:19 — the phrase in its proverbial form is in no verse.
Wikipedia’s Hamlet article ↗ dates composition to 1599–1601 and records the first quarto (Ling and Trundell, 1603), the second quarto (Ling, 1604, some copies 1605) and the First Folio (1623).
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from Project Gutenberg’s Hamlet ↗ (ebook no. 1524). Editions differ on the spelling of the key phrase — Gutenberg prints “to thine own self”, the MIT text “to thine ownself”.

author.name: William Shakespeare
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: c. 1564–1616 · English playwright, poet and actor
author.bio: Shakespeare was baptised in Stratford-upon-Avon on 26 April 1564 and died on 23 April 1616; Wikipedia’s opening line calls him simply “an English playwright, poet and actor.” Hamlet, written around 1599–1601, is the most-quoted play in the language, and Polonius’s farewell speech to Laertes is a dense little anthology of proverbs — “Neither a borrower nor a lender be” and “to thine own self be true” arrive within four lines of each other. Both have long since escaped the play and now circulate as free-floating folk wisdom, which is exactly how one of them ended up filed under Scripture.

misattribution.heading: Where the credit goes wrong
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most persistently “biblical” sentences in English that has never appeared in a Bible. Two separate things get misplaced: the book it came from, and the mouth it came out of.

items.who: Scripture — usually cited as King James, sometimes as Proverbs
items.why: A King James Version search for the string “thine own self” returns just two verses ↗: Exodus 32:13 (“thou swarest by thine own self”) and Philemon 1:19 (“thou owest unto me even thine own self besides”). Neither is the maxim, and neither is about self-fidelity. GotQuestions.org states it plainly ↗: the phrase “is not in the Bible.”

items.who: William Shakespeare, offering personal moral advice
items.why: Shakespeare wrote the line, but he gave it to Polonius — the courtier who spies on his own son, hides behind a tapestry, and is stabbed there. Wikipedia records that he is “described as a windbag by some and a rambler of wisdom by others” ↗. Quoting the sentence as Shakespeare’s own counsel skips over who is talking.

Modern editions do not agree on whether the pronoun and noun are one word or two. Project Gutenberg’s text ↗ prints “to thine own self be true”, while the MIT text of the same scene ↗ prints “to thine ownself be true”. Both are the same line; neither spelling is a different quotation.

misattribution.truthLine: It is Polonius, in Act 1, Scene 3 of Shakespeare’s Hamlet ↗ — a play written around 1599–1601 — and it is in no Bible at all.

context.heading: Why a stage windbag became a devotional motto
lead: Polonius is not a prophet. He is Claudius’s chief counsellor and the play’s most reliable bore — Wikipedia notes he has been “described as a windbag by some and a rambler of wisdom by others” ↗. The advice to Laertes is a rapid-fire string of copybook maxims delivered by a father who spends the rest of the play spying on both of his children, and who dies stabbed through a curtain while eavesdropping. Whether the audience is meant to nod along or wince is one of the play’s oldest arguments.

What is not in dispute is the wording. The precept comes at the end of the speech, immediately after “Neither a borrower nor a lender be” — and the two lines have had very different afterlives. One is remembered as Shakespeare. The other, stripped of its speaker and its irony, drifted far enough from the play to be mistaken for a commandment.
detailsBody: Three things push the line toward the pulpit. The archaic second person — thine, thou canst — is the register English speakers know almost exclusively from the King James Bible, published within a decade of Hamlet. The sentence is built as a moral imperative with a promised consequence (“be true … and it must follow”), the grammatical shape of a proverb or a commandment. And it is quoted almost universally on its own, detached from the character who says it and the scene he says it in.

The confusion is common enough to be answered directly by Bible-reference sites. GotQuestions.org ↗ opens its entry with the flat statement that the phrase is not in the Bible, then sends readers to Hamlet. OpenBible.info ↗ maintains a topical page headed “6 Bible Verses about To Thine Own Self Be True” — and every verse it lists (1 Timothy 6:10, Romans 8:28, Proverbs 3:5 among them) is a thematic neighbour, not a match. The page exists because people go looking; the contents show what they find.
context.pull: Polonius says it, Shakespeare wrote it, and no Bible contains it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Project Gutenberg's Hamlet (ebook 1524) prints, in Polonius's Act 1 Scene 3 speech to Laertes, the line "This above all: to thine own self be true;" followed by "And it must follow, as the night the day, / Thou canst not then be false to any man.", preceded by "Neither a borrower nor a lender be".

The MIT complete-works text of Hamlet Act 1 Scene 3 prints Polonius's precepts speech including "This above all: to thine ownself be true," (compound spelling) through "Farewell: my blessing season this in thee!".
Wikiquote's Hamlet article assigns "This above all: to thine own self be true, / And it must follow, as the night the day, / Thou canst not then be false to any man." to Polonius at Act I, scene iii.
A King James Version search for "to thine own self" at Bible Gateway returns only two verses, Exodus 32:13 and Philemon 1:19; neither contains the maxim "to thine own self be true".
GotQuestions.org states that "To thine own self be true" is not in the Bible and identifies it as advice Polonius gives Laertes in Shakespeare's Hamlet, Act I Scene 3.

OpenBible.info maintains a topical page headed "6 Bible Verses about To Thine Own Self Be True" that lists only thematically related verses (including 1 Timothy 6:10, Romans 8:28 and Proverbs 3:5) and no verse containing the phrase.

Wikipedia's Hamlet article dates the play's composition to between 1599 and 1601, and records the first quarto published by Nicholas Ling and John Trundell in 1603, the second quarto published by Nicholas Ling in 1604 (some copies dated 1605), and the First Folio in 1623.

Wikipedia's Polonius article says Polonius delivers "a list of sententious maxims" to Laertes in Act 1 Scene 3, and that he is "described as a windbag by some and a rambler of wisdom by others"; he is Claudius's chief counsellor and is stabbed by Hamlet behind an arras.
Wikipedia's William Shakespeare article opens "William Shakespeare (c. 23 April 1564 - 23 April 1616) was an English playwright, poet and actor" and notes he was baptised 26 April 1564.
Quote Investigator has no dedicated article investigating "To thine own self be true"; a site search returns only a 2014 article on Shakespeare quotations generally.
